sections.h2: Columbia and the counties behind the bill
sections.html:
Columbia, the capital, counted 136,632 residents in 2020 and is estimated at 147,035 today. The city covers 140.68 square miles and sits mostly in Richland County, with pieces in Lexington and Kershaw counties. Government offices, the University of South Carolina and Fort Jackson anchor local jobs, and that mix supports plenty of rental housing.

Sellers should start with the county line. Whichever county mails your bill supplies the assessor, auditor and treasurer you will phone. Everything below describes Richland County's offices, so a house on the Lexington or Kershaw side needs a call to that county for its own dates and rules.

Richland divides the work among three offices: the Assessor, who assigns value; the Auditor, who computes tax and prepares bills; and the Treasurer, who receives and distributes payments. All three work at 2020 Hampton St., Columbia.

Treasurer hours are weekdays, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Payment is available online, at the counter and by mail, and a monthly plan can be requested. Phone for your current bill and exact due date. Late charges follow state law, which tacks on 3% after January 16, then 7% more by February 2 and 5% more by March 17 (S.C. Code 12-45-180).

sections.h2: How to appeal a Richland County assessment
sections.html:
An appeal begins as a written objection to the Assessor, due 90 days after the date printed on the reassessment notice. In a year with no notice, the cutoff is the first penalty date on that year's real property bill. The statute sets the same 90-day period (S.C. Code 12-60-2510).

An online appeal portal is available. Disputes that the Assessor and taxpayer cannot settle go to the Board of Assessment Appeals. A representative must hold a power of attorney on Form SC2848, and entity-owned property requires articles of organization or an operating agreement.

Paper filings go to 2020 Hampton St., Suite 2058, Columbia, SC 29204. It is worth asking when the next notices will be mailed, since that date can shape when you list.

sections.h2: If you disagree with the value: the paper trail
sections.html:
Good records make an appeal easier. Save the dated reassessment notice, since your 90 days count from that date. Describe the property in your objection, explain what is wrong with the value, and keep a copy that shows when you sent it. Filing through the online portal is fastest.

When an agent, attorney or relative files for you, attach the SC2848 form. When an LLC or similar entity holds title, attach its organizing papers. Incomplete paperwork can stall a filing while your deadline keeps ticking.

A hearing is about value or classification, so bring comparable sales or an appraisal if you have one.

sections.h2: Why Columbia rental owners pay more
sections.html:
South Carolina assesses a home lived in by its owner at 4% and everything else, including rentals and second homes, at 6%. Your bill shows which ratio you have.

The City of Columbia's 2022 competitive property tax plan went further. It put the effective tax rate on commercial and rental property at 2.92% of value in Richland School District One and 3.55% in District Two, and it found that rentals pay 3.9 times more than owner-occupied property. That was a city planning document, not a tax bill, so rely on your actual notice.

A house that stops being a primary residence moves to 6% as well, so an owner who moved out but kept the property may lose the lower rate before listing.

sections.h2: Unpaid taxes and the Richland County tax sale
sections.html:
Taxes left unpaid in Richland County can end at the annual tax sale, normally held in the fall. Recent sales took place at Township Auditorium, 1703 Taylor St., Columbia, with a backup day if the first day ran long.

To halt a sale, pay the whole amount at the Treasurer's office before 5 p.m. on the Friday that precedes it. At that point only cash or a certified bank cashier's check is taken, and personal, company and escrow checks are turned away. Opening bids equal the delinquent taxes and costs plus the current year's taxes, and buyers get the property as is, without warranty.

The redemption period under state law is 12 months from the sale (S.C. Code 12-51-90). Tax sale questions go to delinquenttax@richlandcountysc.gov, and payment plans can be requested at plannedpayment@richlandcountysc.gov.

sections.h2: Selling a Columbia house with taxes owed
sections.html:
Tax owed on a house will not stop a sale. The balance can usually be paid from the proceeds, and the Treasurer can explain payoff timing before you pick a closing date.

  1. Identify the billing county: Richland, Lexington or Kershaw.
  2. Obtain the current bill and a payoff from the Treasurer.
  3. Check whether the house is billed at 4% or 6%.
  4. If the tax sale is close, remember the cash-or-cashier's-check rule.

A cash purchase can close quickly enough to get ahead of a tax sale and spares you repairs and showings. With a rental, an inherited house or an empty property, send us the address and your newest notice and we will say what we can offer.

sections.h2: A short checklist before you list a Columbia house
sections.html:
Settle three questions before the sign goes up. First, the county: a Columbia address may belong to Richland, Lexington or Kershaw, each with separate offices, dates and forms. Second, know the rate. Check your latest bill for either the 4% owner-occupied ratio or the 6% rate that applies to rentals, second homes and former primary residences. Third, know the balance. A Treasurer payoff tells your closing office what to wire, and it avoids a late scramble if the figure has penalties in it.

Buyers and lenders can see the same records, so a clear tax history helps a closing go smoothly.

If a payment plan is on the table, ask for it before the tax sale season rather than during it. The county accepts plan requests by email, and an approved plan gives you a schedule to show a buyer. If you plan to sell instead, ask the Treasurer whether a plan changes the payoff or only the timing, and get the answer in writing for your closing office, with the date it applies.

Finally, remember who may need to sign the paperwork. For an entity-owned or inherited house, the person who deals with the Assessor or Treasurer needs proof of authority, which usually means the same organizing papers or power of attorney the appeal process asks for.

faqs.q: Which county do I pay property tax to if I live in Columbia?
faqs.a: Most of Columbia lies in Richland County, so the Richland County Treasurer bills you. Some parcels sit in Lexington or Kershaw counties, and your bill names the one that applies.

faqs.q: How long do I have to appeal my Richland County assessment?
faqs.a: Ninety days, counted from the date on the reassessment notice, to send the Assessor a written objection. If no notice went out, the deadline is that year's first penalty date.

faqs.q: Does Richland County offer a property tax payment plan?
faqs.a: Yes. A monthly plan can be requested through the county's property tax page, and plannedpayment@richlandcountysc.gov handles those requests.

faqs.q: Can I stop a Richland County tax sale?
faqs.a: Yes, if you pay everything owed before 5 p.m. on the Friday ahead of the sale. Only cash or a certified bank cashier's check is taken then.

faqs.q: Why is my Columbia rental taxed at 6%?
faqs.a: A rental, second home or vacant house misses the 4% legal residence rate, and the state assesses that property at 6%.
